front: The lesson names four Christian responses to the problem of evil. What are they?
answer: Free will / Life as a test / Part of God's plan / The Devil
title: The Nature of God & the Trinity

front: What are the three persons of the Trinity?
answer: Father / Son (Jesus Christ) / Holy Spirit
title: The Nature of God & the Trinity

front: How does the story of Job support the idea that suffering can test faith?
answer: It shows God allows suffering to test whether people remain faithful, and rewards those who do.
title: The Nature of God & the Trinity

front: Why don't Christians see the Trinity as three separate gods?
answer: Because the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are all fully God, sharing one divine nature.
title: The Nature of God & the Trinity

front: The lesson describes three Christian views on interpreting the creation account in Genesis. What are they?
answer: Literalist view / Liberal view / Catholic view
title: Creation, the Afterlife & Judgement

front: How does the Catholic Church explain evolution and the Big Bang alongside belief in God as creator?
answer: It teaches that faith and science are not in conflict; God is behind the Big Bang and evolution.
title: Creation, the Afterlife & Judgement

front: Why do Catholics pray for people who have died?
answer: To ask God to release their souls from purgatory sooner, so they can enter heaven.
title: Creation, the Afterlife & Judgement

front: The lesson says Jesus's life follows a connected sequence of four events. What are they, in order?
answer: Incarnation / Crucifixion / Resurrection / Ascension
title: Incarnation, Crucifixion & Resurrection

front: Why is the incarnation necessary for salvation, according to Christian belief?
answer: Because only someone who was both fully God and fully human could bridge the gap between a holy God and sinful humanity.
title: Incarnation, Crucifixion & Resurrection

front: How does the resurrection give Christians hope for their own future?
answer: It shows God has power over death, giving Christians hope that they too will one day be resurrected.
title: Incarnation, Crucifixion & Resurrection

front: The lesson names three ways Christians believe salvation happens. What are they?
answer: Law / Grace / The Holy Spirit
title: Sin, Salvation & Atonement

front: The lesson gives three understandings of atonement. What are they?
answer: Substitutionary atonement / Satisfaction theory / Moral example
title: Sin, Salvation & Atonement

front: How does satisfaction theory explain Jesus's death differently from substitutionary atonement?
answer: Substitutionary atonement says Jesus took humanity's punishment; satisfaction theory says his death paid a debt to restore God's offended honour.
title: Sin, Salvation & Atonement

front: Why might a liberal Christian see Jesus's death primarily as a moral example rather than a payment for sin?
answer: Because they see it as a supreme act of self-sacrificing love that inspires Christians to live selflessly for others.
title: Sin, Salvation & Atonement

front: The lesson names four main ways Christians worship. What are they?
answer: Liturgical / Non-liturgical / Informal / Private
title: Worship and Prayer

front: The prayer acronym STOP stands for four reasons Christians pray. What are they?
answer: Sorry (confession) / Thank (gratitude) / Others (intercession) / Please (petition)
title: Worship and Prayer

front: Why is the Lord's Prayer considered a model for how Christians should pray?
answer: Because it combines praise of God, submission to his will, requests for daily needs, and forgiveness.
title: Worship and Prayer

front: Why is private worship valuable to Christians, even though they also worship together?
answer: It gives personal time with God away from everyday pressures, building a relationship communal worship may not provide.
title: Worship and Prayer

front: The lesson names three churches that practise infant baptism. Which are they?
answer: Roman Catholic / Anglican / Methodist
title: The Sacraments: Baptism and Holy Communion

front: The lesson gives four different Christian views on Holy Communion. What are they?
answer: Catholic - transubstantiation / Orthodox - Divine Liturgy / Protestant - symbolic remembrance / Salvation Army & Quakers - no Communion
title: The Sacraments: Baptism and Holy Communion

front: Why do the Salvation Army and Quakers not practise Holy Communion?
answer: They believe Christ's presence does not depend on physical elements, and that every meal can be sacred.
title: The Sacraments: Baptism and Holy Communion

front: Why do Catholics see receiving the Eucharist as essential for spiritual life?
answer: Because Jesus taught that without eating his flesh and drinking his blood, a person has no life in them.
title: The Sacraments: Baptism and Holy Communion

front: The lesson names four days of Holy Week leading to Easter. What are they, in order?
answer: Palm Sunday / Maundy Thursday / Good Friday / Easter Sunday
title: Pilgrimage and Celebrations

front: Why are some Christians critical of the idea of going on pilgrimage?
answer: They believe God can be worshipped anywhere, and that money spent travelling could instead help the poor.
title: Pilgrimage and Celebrations

front: Why do some Christians worry that the true meaning of Christmas is being lost today?
answer: They feel commercialism and shopping have overshadowed the religious focus on Jesus's birth and its meaning.
title: Pilgrimage and Celebrations

front: The lesson names three worldwide Christian charities that respond to poverty and disaster. What are they?
answer: CAFOD / Christian Aid / Tearfund
title: The Church in the Local Community

front: The lesson names four ways churches respond to the persecution of Christians worldwide. What are they?
answer: Praying for persecuted Christians / Raising awareness / Campaigning for religious freedom / Providing practical support
title: The Church in the Local Community

front: Why do CAFOD, Christian Aid and Tearfund all carry out charitable work?
answer: They are all motivated by Jesus's teaching to love your neighbour and care for the poor.
title: The Church in the Local Community

front: Why do churches see running or supporting food banks as an expression of their Christian faith?
answer: Because Jesus taught that helping someone who is hungry is the same as serving God himself.
title: The Church in the Local Community

front: The lesson names four organisations that support Christian mission and evangelism. What are they?
answer: The Alpha Course / The Church Army / Christ for all Nations (CfaN) / Fresh Expressions of Church
title: Mission, Evangelism and World Poverty

front: The lesson names three Christian charities that respond to world poverty. What are they?
answer: CAFOD / Tearfund / Christian Aid
title: Mission, Evangelism and World Poverty

front: Why is the instruction to baptise new converts significant in the Great Commission?
answer: It shows that baptism has been central to the Church's mission from the very beginning.
title: Mission, Evangelism and World Poverty

front: Why does the Church's mission involve more than just evangelism?
answer: Because making disciples means evangelism must be followed by training new converts to follow Jesus and spread the faith.
title: Mission, Evangelism and World Poverty

front: Sunni Islam has six Articles of Faith. What are they?
answer: Tawhid (oneness of Allah) / Malaikah (angels) / Kutub (holy books) / Risalah (prophethood) / Akhirah (afterlife) / Al-Qadr (predestination)
title: Key Beliefs: Sunni and Shi'a Islam

front: Shi'a Islam has five Roots of Usul ad-Din. What are they?
answer: Tawhid (oneness of Allah) / Adalat (justice) / Nubuwwah (prophethood) / Imamate (leadership) / Al-Ma'ad (resurrection)
title: Key Beliefs: Sunni and Shi'a Islam

front: Why did Islam split into Sunni and Shi'a branches after Muhammad's death?
answer: Muslims disagreed over who should lead the community after Muhammad died in 632 CE.
title: Key Beliefs: Sunni and Shi'a Islam

front: Why do Sunni and Shi'a Muslims still share the same fundamental faith despite their differences?
answer: Their differences stem from a dispute over leadership, not belief — both worship the same God and follow the same Qur'an.
title: Key Beliefs: Sunni and Shi'a Islam

front: The lesson names four key qualities of Allah's nature. What are they?
answer: Omnipotence (Al-Qadir) / Beneficence (Ar-Rahman) / Mercy (Ar-Rahim) / Fairness and justice (Al-Adl)
title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah and Angels

front: The lesson names four roles angels perform in Muslim life. What are they?
answer: Deliver revelations to prophets / Record good and bad deeds / Welcome the righteous into paradise / Be present at the Day of Judgement
items: Be present at the Day of Judgement
title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah and Angels

front: Why can Allah be both transcendent and immanent without contradiction, in Muslim belief?
answer: Allah is powerful enough to be beyond the universe and yet closer to a person than their jugular vein.
title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah and Angels

front: Why does belief in recording angels encourage Muslims to behave morally each day?
answer: Knowing that an angel is recording every deed acts as a powerful deterrent against doing wrong.
title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah and Angels

front: The lesson names five holy books revealed to different prophets in Islam. What are they?
answer: Qur'an / Torah (Tawrat) / Psalms (Zabur) / Gospel (Injil) / Scrolls of Abraham (Suhuf Ibrahim)
title: Prophethood and the Holy Books

front: The lesson focuses on three key prophets in Islam. Who are they?
answer: Adam / Ibrahim (Abraham) / Muhammad
title: Prophethood and the Holy Books

front: Why is Adam not seen as carrying 'original sin' in Islamic belief?
answer: Because Allah accepted his sincere repentance, so every person after him is instead born sinless.
title: Prophethood and the Holy Books

front: Why do senior Shi'a scholars hold religious authority today, even though the twelfth Imam is in hiding?
answer: Because the Imam is in hiding, scholars act as his representatives, interpreting Islamic law on his behalf.
title: Prophethood and the Holy Books

front: The lesson says an angel records four things about a person's life before they are born. What are they?
answer: Provision (livelihood) / Lifespan / Deeds / Whether they will be happy or unhappy
items: Whether they will be happy or unhappy
title: Predestination and Human Responsibility

front: The lesson names four qualities that a sense of accountability encourages in Muslims. What are they?
answer: Honesty / Generosity / Compassion / Obedience to Allah
title: Predestination and Human Responsibility

front: Why can't a Muslim blame family, friends or fate for their own wrongdoing?
answer: Because no one can carry another person's sins — each person answers for the choices they freely make.
title: Predestination and Human Responsibility

front: The lesson gives four reasons a person may be sent to Jahannam. What are they?
answer: Living a wicked, evil life / Rejecting the Qur'an's teachings / Refusing to take responsibility, blaming others / Committing shirk
items: Refusing to take responsibility, blaming others
title: Akhirah: Life After Death

front: Why can Jahannam serve as a place of purification for some sinful believers, rather than permanent punishment?
answer: Allah may use it to purify sinful believers, then move them on into Jannah when He chooses.
title: Akhirah: Life After Death

front: Why is Allah's judgement of a person considered fair, even though Allah already knows what they will do?
answer: Because Allah gave humans free will, making them responsible and accountable for the choices they made.
title: Akhirah: Life After Death

front: Sunni Islam has Five Pillars. What are they?
answer: Shahadah / Salah / Zakah / Sawm / Hajj
title: The Five Pillars, the Ten Obligatory Acts and Shahadah

front: Beyond the Five Pillars they share with Sunnis, Shi'a Muslims add six further duties. What are they?
answer: Khums (tax on surplus income) / Jihad (striving in God's way) / Amr bil ma'ruf (commanding good) / Nahi anil munkar (forbidding evil) / Tawalla (loving the Prophet's family) / Tabarra (rejecting their enemies)
title: The Five Pillars, the Ten Obligatory Acts and Shahadah

front: Why does neglecting one of the Five Pillars weaken a Muslim's whole spiritual life?
answer: Because each pillar supports the others, and together they form a complete framework for living by Allah's will.
title: The Five Pillars, the Ten Obligatory Acts and Shahadah

front: Why is Khums considered a particularly important duty within the Ten Obligatory Acts?
answer: Because the money partly supports Muhammad's descendants and the religious scholars who guide the Shi'a community.
title: The Five Pillars, the Ten Obligatory Acts and Shahadah

front: The lesson names the five daily prayers Sunni Muslims perform, in order. What are they?
answer: Fajr (before sunrise) / Zuhr (just after midday) / Asr (afternoon) / Maghrib (just after sunset) / Isha (night)
title: Salah and Sawm

front: Wudu involves washing or wiping six parts of the body, in order. What are they?
answer: Hands / Mouth and nose / Face / Forearms to the elbows / Head and ears (wiped) / Feet to the ankles
title: Salah and Sawm

front: Why do many Muslims spend the whole of Laylat al-Qadr in prayer?
answer: Because they believe worship on this night earns a greater reward than a thousand months of ordinary worship.
title: Salah and Sawm

front: Why does Jummah, the Friday prayer, matter for the Muslim community as a whole?
answer: It strengthens the ummah by bringing Muslims together in one place as a community every week.
title: Salah and Sawm

front: The lesson says Zakah has three purposes. What are they?
answer: Purifies the giver from greed / Supports those in genuine need / Reduces inequality in the ummah
title: Zakah and Hajj

front: The lesson names six key rituals of Hajj, in order. What are they?
answer: Tawaf (circling the Ka'aba) / Sa'i (between Safa and Marwa) / Arafat (standing in prayer) / Muzdalifah (praying, collecting pebbles) / Mina (stoning the pillars) / Sacrifice (Qurbani)
title: Zakah and Hajj

front: Why is Zakah not simply charity in the ordinary sense?
answer: Because it is a compulsory duty for every Muslim above the nisab threshold, not a voluntary choice.
title: Zakah and Hajj

front: Why do pilgrims wear simple white garments (ihram) during Hajj?
answer: They symbolise equality before God, stripping away distinctions of wealth, status and nationality.
title: Zakah and Hajj

front: Islamic teaching sets five conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared. What are they?
answer: Must be defensive / Must be a last resort / Declared by a recognised authority / Must be proportionate / Must stop when the enemy seeks peace
items: Must stop when the enemy seeks peace
title: Jihad

front: Why can only defensive wars count as lesser jihad, not wars of conquest?
answer: Because lesser jihad is only permitted to protect Islam, Muslim lands or oppressed people, never for territory or personal gain.
title: Jihad

front: Why must peaceful options be tried before lesser jihad can be declared?
answer: Because all peaceful means, such as negotiation, diplomacy and treaties, must be exhausted first, since it is only a last resort.
title: Jihad

front: Qurbani meat at Eid al-Adha is divided into three equal portions. Who are they for?
answer: The family / Friends and neighbours / The poor
title: Festivals and Commemorations

front: This lesson covers three Muslim festivals and commemorations. What are they?
answer: Eid al-Fitr / Eid al-Adha / Ashura
title: Festivals and Commemorations

front: Why did Husayn refuse to pledge allegiance to Yazid?
answer: He believed Yazid was religiously misguided and that the promise to keep leadership within the Prophet's family had been broken.
title: Festivals and Commemorations

front: Why do Sunni and Shi'a Muslims commemorate Ashura in such different ways?
answer: They commemorate different events: Shi'a mourn Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala, while Sunnis recall Musa's escape through the Red Sea.
title: Festivals and Commemorations

front: The lesson names four purposes of marriage. What are they?
answer: Lifelong companionship / A stable environment for children / Sexual intimacy within commitment / Following God's plan
title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce

front: Why is there a three-month waiting period (iddah) after a divorce in Islam?
answer: To allow time for reconciliation and to check whether the wife is pregnant.
title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce

front: Why do most Protestant churches accept divorce despite Jesus's teaching against separating what God has joined?
answer: They accept it as a last resort, showing compassion for people in unhappy or abusive marriages.
title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce

front: The lesson gives four religious arguments for gender equality. What are they?
answer: Both created in God's image / Galatians 3:28: spiritual equality / Qur'an 33:35: equal rewards / Jesus treated women with respect
title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality

front: The lesson names three purposes of family life. What are they?
answer: Procreation / Stability and protection / Educating children in a faith
title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality

front: Why do some Christians argue that men and women should have different roles, not identical ones?
answer: They believe the Bible teaches husbands should be head of the family, and women should not have authority over men.
title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality

front: Why do many Muslims argue that Islam was ahead of its time on women's rights?
answer: Because it gave women the right to own property, inherit and divorce centuries before Western law did.
title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality

front: The lesson gives three contrasting views on same-sex relationships. What are they?
answer: Conservative Christians oppose them / Liberal Christians accept them / Islam opposes them
title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships

front: The lesson gives three situations in which many Muslim scholars accept contraception within marriage. What are they?
answer: Pregnancy would harm the mother's health / The family cannot afford more children / It would protect existing children's welfare
items: Pregnancy would harm the mother's health
The family cannot afford more children
It would protect existing children's welfare
title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships

front: Why do some Islamic scholars oppose contraception, even within marriage?
answer: Because they believe children are a blessing from Allah, and humans should not interfere with God's will.
title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships

front: Why do liberal Christians believe the Bible's teaching should not be used to oppose same-sex relationships today?
answer: They argue the Bible must be read in its historical context, and that Jesus taught love for all people.
title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships

front: The lesson names six types of family. What are they?
answer: Nuclear / Extended / Single-parent / Blended (step) / Same-sex parent / Polygamous
title: Families and Contemporary Family Issues

front: The lesson names three key purposes of family life. What are they?
answer: Procreation / Stability and protection of children / Educating children in a faith
title: Families and Contemporary Family Issues

front: Why does the Bible warn fathers against being too harsh with their children?
answer: Because being too hard on children can cause them to become discouraged.
title: Families and Contemporary Family Issues

front: Why is the extended family considered the basis of Islamic society?
answer: Because it is part of God's plan for people, and it shapes the moral values and character of children.
title: Families and Contemporary Family Issues

front: Why do some Muslim women in Britain face prejudice that can affect their employment?
answer: Many face prejudice because of the way they dress, for example wearing the hijab.
title: Gender Equality, Prejudice and Discrimination

front: Why can some Christians support different roles for men and women while still believing they are equal?
answer: They see it as fair to treat men and women differently if that reflects God's will, while still viewing them as equal.
title: Gender Equality, Prejudice and Discrimination

front: Genesis 1 describes God creating six things, in order. What are they?
answer: Light / Sky / Land / Plants / Animals / Humans
title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life

front: Why do many non-literal Christians see the Big Bang as compatible with Genesis?
answer: Because the order of creation in Genesis broadly matches the order of events described by science.
title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life

front: Why do some creationists argue the Big Bang still points to a creator?
answer: Because the Big Bang cannot explain what existed before it or what caused it, suggesting a creator was needed.
title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life

front: The lesson names five ways humans use animals. What are they?
answer: Food / Clothing / Medical research / Entertainment / Companionship
title: The Environment & Animal Rights

front: Why is saving a human life given such high priority when some Muslim scholars permit animal experimentation?
answer: Because the Qur'an teaches that saving one life is like saving the whole of humanity.
title: The Environment & Animal Rights

front: Why do many Christians choose to eat less meat or become vegetarian, even though Christianity has no dietary laws?
answer: Out of concern for animal welfare and the environment, even though their faith sets no dietary rules.
title: The Environment & Animal Rights

front: The lesson names three types of euthanasia / assisted dying. What are they?
answer: Voluntary euthanasia / Non-voluntary euthanasia / Assisted suicide
title: Abortion & Euthanasia

front: Why does the principle of double effect allow a procedure that indirectly causes a foetus's death?
answer: Because the intended outcome is saving the mother's life; the foetus's death is an unintended side effect.
title: Abortion & Euthanasia

front: Why do most Muslim scholars treat abortion differently before and after 120 days of pregnancy?
answer: Because they believe the soul enters the body (ensoulment) at 120 days, making abortion more seriously wrong after that.
title: Abortion & Euthanasia

front: The lesson names three other religious views on the afterlife, beyond Christianity and Islam. What are they?
answer: Hindus and Sikhs: reincarnation / Buddhists: rebirth without a permanent soul / Judaism: no single fixed view
items: Buddhists: rebirth without a permanent soul
title: Death and an Afterlife

front: Why do some Catholics believe in both the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the body?
answer: They believe the soul lives on after death, then is reunited with a resurrected body at the end of time.
title: Death and an Afterlife

front: Why might someone who believes in reincarnation be motivated to live a good life now?
answer: They believe good actions in this life (karma) lead to a better next life through reincarnation.
title: Death and an Afterlife

front: Why did Martin Luther King Jr go to prison rather than use force during the civil rights movement?
answer: He chose non-violent protest to fight for civil rights, accepting prison rather than resorting to violence.
title: Peace, Justice & Forgiveness

front: Why do some Christians accept that violence may sometimes be a last resort?
answer: They see it as acceptable only once all peaceful options have been tried and have failed.
title: Peace, Justice & Forgiveness

front: The lesson names three main reasons wars begin. What are they?
answer: Greed / Self-defence / Retaliation
title: War: Just War, Holy War & Pacifism

front: The lesson gives four conditions for a holy war to be legitimate in Islam. What are they?
answer: Declared by a recognised religious authority / Fought in self-defence, not aggression / Uses proportionate force / Does not target civilians
items: Declared by a recognised religious authority
title: War: Just War, Holy War & Pacifism

front: How does a holy war differ from a just war, according to the lesson?
answer: A just war is judged by moral criteria and need not be religious; a holy war is fought for a religious cause.
title: War: Just War, Holy War & Pacifism

front: Why do most Christian and Muslim leaders today reject the idea of holy war?
answer: They argue that religion should not be used to justify violence.
title: War: Just War, Holy War & Pacifism

front: The lesson names three types of weapons of mass destruction. What are they?
answer: Nuclear weapons / Biological weapons / Chemical weapons
title: Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction

front: Why do some interpret Islamic teaching as allowing a country to possess nuclear weapons for defence?
answer: They interpret self-defence teaching as allowing possession of such weapons for defence, though not offensive use against civilians.
title: Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction

front: Why do critics of nuclear deterrence say it makes the world less safe, not more?
answer: They say it wastes huge amounts of money and increases the risk of terrorists obtaining such weapons.
title: Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction

front: The lesson names six kinds of people or things war creates victims of. What are they?
answer: Those who fight / Families / Children / Civilians in war-torn areas / Refugees / The land itself
title: Peacemaking and Responses to Victims of War

front: The lesson names four ways Christians may respond to victims of war. What are they?
answer: Praying for victims / Campaigning their government for support / Helping victims directly / Giving money to charities
title: Peacemaking and Responses to Victims of War

front: Why does the Prophet Muhammad's treatment of prisoners of war matter for how Muslims should treat war's victims?
answer: It shows that even enemies deserve humane treatment, setting an example for Muslims to follow.
title: Peacemaking and Responses to Victims of War

front: Why do Muslims feel a responsibility to support fellow Muslims suffering because of war, wherever they live?
answer: Because the ummah is a global community, Muslims feel responsible for supporting fellow believers across national borders.
title: Peacemaking and Responses to Victims of War

front: The lesson names four main categories of reasons people commit crime. What are they?
answer: Poverty and upbringing / Mental health and addiction / Greed and hate / Opposition to unjust laws
title: Good, Evil & Reasons for Crime

front: The lesson names three specific types of crime it covers. What are they?
answer: Hate crimes / Theft / Murder
title: Good, Evil & Reasons for Crime

front: Why might someone who breaks an unjust law, like Rosa Parks, be seen as morally right by religious believers?
answer: Because many religious believers accept that an immoral law can be legitimately opposed.
title: Good, Evil & Reasons for Crime

front: Why do Christians try to separate the sinner from the sin when responding to crime?
answer: Because Jesus himself spent time with sinners and outcasts, showing that people need compassion, not just condemnation.
title: Good, Evil & Reasons for Crime

front: The lesson names three main aims of punishment. What are they?
answer: Retribution / Deterrence / Reformation
title: Punishment: Aims, Types & the Death Penalty

front: The lesson describes three ways criminals can be punished, besides the death penalty. What are they?
answer: Prison / Corporal punishment / Community service
title: Punishment: Aims, Types & the Death Penalty

front: How does the Parable of the Lost Son support the idea that criminals can be redeemed?
answer: It shows God welcoming back those who have strayed, suggesting people who do wrong can still be redeemed.
title: Punishment: Aims, Types & the Death Penalty

front: Why might the principle of utility be used to support the death penalty?
answer: If it deters crime and protects society, it produces the greatest good for the greatest number of people.
title: Punishment: Aims, Types & the Death Penalty

front: The lesson gives three real-world examples of forgiveness after violence. What are they?
answer: Gee Walker (Anthony Walker's mother) / The Truth and Reconciliation Commission / The Amish school shooting (2006)
title: Forgiveness

front: Why did Archbishop Desmond Tutu believe forgiveness and truth-telling could heal South Africa better than punishment?
answer: He believed forgiveness and truth-telling would heal a divided nation more effectively than punishment.
title: Forgiveness

front: Why can someone forgive a criminal while still supporting them facing a prison sentence?
answer: Because forgiveness and justice serve different purposes — forgiveness is personal, while justice holds people accountable.
title: Forgiveness

front: The lesson gives four arguments in favour of the death penalty. What are they?
answer: Deterrence / Retribution / Protection / Cost
title: The Death Penalty

front: The lesson gives five arguments against the death penalty. What are they?
answer: Innocent people could be killed / No chance for reformation / It is inhumane / It does not deter crime / It contradicts the law on murder
items: It contradicts the law on murder
title: The Death Penalty

front: Why do some argue that executing a criminal makes the state no better than the murderer?
answer: Because if killing is wrong, the state commits the same act it is punishing by killing the criminal.
title: The Death Penalty

front: Why does the sanctity of life argument say the death penalty is like 'playing God'?
answer: Because God created all life, so only God has the right to take it away.
title: The Death Penalty
